We said what our opponents said — word for word, creed for creed. Nobody in Africa called the other side heretics, because nobody could. The quarrel was never about who Christ is. It was about who may hand on what he gave.

But what we kept nearest shows up wherever our own people speak at length. When an imperial judge at Carthage courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

The good news, as we told it, ran along the same line. A church is not known by whose favour it enjoys. When the argument at Carthage finally reached the Scriptures, our own bishop of Caesarea answered verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you. Read that in a town with two bishops and an emperor backing one of them, and it is not a devotional sentiment. It is a test, and we thought we could pass it.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. Our own martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. And a bishop writing to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death closed by telling them plainly that the same might yet be asked of any of them. That is our gospel in its working form: he stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us - it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So when you ask what we had of Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian - our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

As for how we knew the resurrection happened: we will not manufacture an answer for you. No writing of ours arguing that case has survived. What survived is what we did with it. We buried our dead inside the walls of the basilica where they were killed, kept the day they died, and read the account of each death aloud again every year, as though the ending were not the end. That is an answer of a kind. It is not the kind you asked for.

We would not call that the question. What we can show you is a day and a threshold: the washing, done in public, where everyone could see which building you walked into. Belief, in our practice, did not happen privately first and publicly after. It was a public act with a date on it.

The question we pressed was not whether a soul believed hard enough. It was whose hand would go into the water with that soul. What we look to is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. Whatever you have done, it was never your record that was on trial at our font. It was ours.

And when our own council condemned men in the harshest words it had - language about shipwrecked bodies covering the shore, unable even to find burial - and then took two of those same men back into office without repeating anything, the door proved wider than our own doctrine put it.

So if you are saying you cannot make yourself believe, we would not tell you that was the wrong place to start. We would tell you the place we know how to begin: not in a private feeling examined first, but at a font, where a trustworthy hand gives what it has to give.

On Christ himself we said what our opponents said. Word for word, creed for creed. Nobody in Africa called the other side heretics, because nobody could. The quarrel was never about who Christ is. It was about who may hand on what he gave.

Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God — we held that as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting held it, and in the same Latin words. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

Here is where you will find us poorer than you expect. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors — one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.

Tyconius, a layman among us, wrote seven rules for reading scripture. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. His book went on to shape the rival church's own way of reading.

The defining question among us was never who Jesus is. It was whose hand can be trusted to give what he gave. Everything else follows from that.

We held standard North African Latin Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God -- we held that as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting held it, and in the same Latin words. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

What we can tell you about the nature of God is not a developed teaching we left behind. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors -- one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.

We cannot show you treatises on God's essence, or arguments about his attributes worked out across generations. What we can show you is where we met him: Our own texts say so without embarrassment. The night before he faced the proconsul, one of our martyrs saw the wine in his cup take the shape of a ring shining with blood and light. That night he dreamed he fought the emperor himself and was crowned by a bright youth. Another was shown a cup, a crown and a palm while he fasted at the top of the cliff he was about to be thrown from. Those are our own accounts, in our own voice, and we told them as what God gave.

This is the limit of what we held in common and can show you directly. Beyond that creed, our energy went elsewhere.

A council of bishops decided, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

You can check almost all of it, which is rarer than you think. The proceedings survive - the acts of the council at Cirta, the sentences from Cebarsussi and Bagai, and above all the transcript of the great conference at Carthage, where an imperial notary took down every word for three days.

Now the harder piece. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors - one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead. We held one creed with the church we fought, word for word, and the split was never about God or grace or the bread. It was about one thing. Whose hand may give what the church gives. We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over.

So when you ask who settled doctrine, the honest answer is that we did not argue doctrine the way you mean it. We argued legitimacy - whose ordination counted, whose hands were clean - and councils settled that. The great eastern councils of that century are not our fight and do not appear in our record; every council our own bishops sat in was about one question, which was who the true church is, and none of them was about who Christ is.

We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned was never actually our fight. Go and read the whole enormous argument between us and the other side and you will find it never once turns on whether the bishop who handed the scriptures over was sorry afterwards. That was not the hinge. The hinge was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. So a man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain, because those are two different questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second.

You can hear what that costs. It means an unrepentant man is not owed your trust merely because you owe him no grudge. And it means the reverse too: you can genuinely let go of the anger and still refuse to hand him the thing he broke. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

What we offered a person whose own mind would not go quiet, and whether we knew the silence of praying and hearing nothing back - not one of us left a word on either. It is not that our people had no inner life. It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.

We were not reading for comfort or for doctrine. We were reading for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings.

Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside.

Our own bishop of Caesarea was doing exactly that when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God - Deo laudes - and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

We read combatively, and about one subject. On the third day at Carthage the bishop of Hippo argued from the wheat and the tares that a church holds good and bad together, and that what is to be saved is the world. Our own bishop of Caesarea answered him out of the same books, verse against verse - the world did not know him; every mouth stopped and all guilty before God; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. That is our reading in one exchange. We went to the text for a test of which of two visible churches was the true one, and we found the church described as the party the world hates rather than the party it favours.

A historian would ask you one question about everything we have told you, and it is the right question: who wrote it down? The answer, for nearly all of it, is our enemies. Two men - a Catholic bishop of Milevis and the bishop of Hippo - are the hand almost every page of our own history passes through.

Our best theologian's letters survive chopped into clauses inside the book written to demolish them. The fullest account of our founding decade is a polemic aimed at proving us wrong. When you hear us tell a story with rich detail, ask first whether the detail is ours or the detail of a man who needed it to land a blow.

But the founding documents run the other way, and they do not flatter us. There is a court transcript in which a notary confesses, under threat of torture, that he forged the letter proving our central accusation, and that he did it working for our side. There is another in which our own bishops are read out advising each other, in writing, to keep a charge out of court because it was true. We could not remove those if we wanted to. They are the most checkable things we have.

Four things escape that, and only four, and each is short. A sermon preached at a martyr's grave. A passion of one of our bishops. One bishop's own letter to his own congregation. And one book of interpretation by a man our own council condemned. Add to that the transcript of the great conference, where a notary took our bishops down verbatim with no adversary choosing which words to keep - and note that the copy of it we can actually reach is the worst-damaged text in this whole corpus.

There is one thing nobody mediated at all. On two pillars near Bagai, and on three other stones, two words are cut: Deo laudes. Praise to God. That is our voice with no enemy between you and it, and it is two words long. We know our own shout better than we know the room we shouted it in.

No, and the evidence for that is what our opponents had to say to beat us. Our case ran on two legs. One was scripture. The other was Carthage: eighty-seven African bishops, sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing again the people who came to us from the other communion, we were not producing a novelty from a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding, and among us the something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

Two bishops for one city, across all of Roman North Africa - where our rival has a bishop, so do we, and at the great Conference at Carthage, 279 of our bishops sat facing 286 of theirs. That is not a movement. That is one whole church facing another whole church, see for see, down to towns no one has heard of.

Our senior bishop sits at Carthage - Donatus held it, then Parmenian, then Primian. Our rival claims the same see for its own man at the same time, so there are two primates in one city, as there are two bishops in every town.

Our bishops govern by council, as any true church does, and that our councils could judge and discipline our own dissidents is part of our claim to be one. Cebarsussi elected a rival primate in 393; Bagai condemned him the year after. A council is not an advisory board among us. Our own council at Bagai took the Maximianist clergy back, without baptizing them again or ordaining them again. That is a church governing itself.

How a man comes to hold office is both together: the people and the bishops. We can show you what that looked like when it went wrong. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back - let it be another; hear us, God - and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be overridden. It could not be ignored.

# Underground concealment

Nobody among us hid underground. The persecutions in our own time did not send us into tunnels; they sent soldiers into our buildings in broad daylight, under orders, to enforce a single church.

We read the account of one such day aloud every year: a basilica at Carthage seized, a house of prayer turned into a place of feasting and licence, people clubbed to death where they knelt with their eyes shut, and buried inside the walls because there was nowhere else and nobody to stop it. That is what persecution looked like for us. Not hiding. Being visited.

The picture of catacombs belongs to a different church at a different time. Our persecution came as soldiers sent into our buildings in daylight, under orders. What was taken from us were basilicas we already held openly, in towns where both communions stood visible to each other and to the state.

Three answers, and they do not agree.

Our founding bishops sat at Cirta, before any of this hardened, and Secundus of Tigisis put the question to them: had any of them, under the persecution, handed over the scriptures? One by one, several admitted that they had. Then Purpurius turned the question back on Secundus himself, taunting him, and the room began to mutter that he too must have given up the sacred books to buy his own release.

Secundus took advice from his own brother's son, who counselled him to remit the whole affair to God rather than press it further. Secundus then turned to the three bishops present who had not themselves been accused and asked their judgement. They answered that a case of this kind ought to be reserved to the Lord. Sit down, all, Secundus said. Thanks be to God, the assembly answered, and did. No one present was found guilty; no one was cleared. The room simply agreed not to finish the question it had started.

The men who would spend the next century insisting a bishop's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real found the question unanswerable about themselves, within the hour, and stopped.

In 393 a deacon named Maximian was elected as a rival primate at Cebarsussi, in direct defiance of Primian. A much larger council - three hundred and ten bishops - met at Bagai in 394 and condemned the Maximianists in language that did not soften what it meant: shipwrecked men dashed by the waves of truth upon the sharp rocks, their bodies covering the shore, so thoroughly that they fail to find so much as burial. And then, having said this, the council did something its own decree's language did nothing to prepare a listener for. When Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuris, two of the condemned Maximianist bishops, were brought back into the fold, it was done without rebaptism and without reordination. A general named Optatus Gildonianus enforced the reconciliation with military force. The very men whose ordination the council had just described in the imagery of shipwreck and unburied death were received back into full office, exactly as they had been ordained under the schism the council had just condemned in the harshest terms it had.

Tyconius made an argument from Scripture too well supported to simply dismiss. He argued, at length and with abundant scriptural support, that the Christians of Africa belonged to a church spread across the whole earth. Anyone actually listening to the case he built could see where it led: those who had cut themselves off from that communion were the ones who had separated themselves from something real. Parmenian, our own bishop at Carthage, and the leaders around him saw exactly where the argument pointed. Parmenian wrote to Tyconius directly, rebuking him for preaching that the church extended across the whole earth, and warning him not to dare do it again. Tyconius did not recant, and did not leave. He kept arguing what he had argued, from inside the party that had told him to stop.

It is reported that Tyconius was afterward condemned by a council of his own communion. He was never received back. He did not go over to the other side either. He simply remained, for whatever years he had left, the head of a schismatic church so small that he may have been the only one left in it.

Three ways we responded when our own failed or pressed us. The first was to reserve the matter to the Lord and sit down together. The second was to condemn in the harshest words we had, and then quietly

No continuous line to any present-day communion is documented at any point. This is not a living tradition today: no church now living holds a documented line back to it.

The quarrel outlived the empire that fed it and went on for a century and a half more under new masters, and a bishop of Rome was still writing letters about rebaptism in Numidia nearly three hundred years after our founding. Then the record simply stops. No line runs from us to any communion you could walk into now.

Walk it through. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over.

What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient - so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Now the step before that. How did someone who could not read receive any of it? By standing still and listening, on a fixed day, in a particular place. Every year, on the day one of our own died, we gathered at the grave and the account of that death was read out loud again. That is how the words came to most of us: aloud, at a graveside, on an anniversary, to people who could not check a single detail and came anyway.

The washing was the threshold. What came before it was hearing - the martyrs' own accounts, read at the grave each year. What came after was belonging to the body whose hand could be trusted to give what it gave.

We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage. Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all - so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority - that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned was never actually our fight. Go and read the whole enormous argument between us and the other side and you will find it never once turns on whether the bishop who handed the scriptures over was sorry afterwards. That was not the hinge. The hinge was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. So a man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain, because those are two different questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second.

It means an unrepentant man is not owed your trust merely because you owe him no grudge. And it means the reverse too: you can genuinely let go of the anger and still refuse to hand him the thing he broke. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

For someone whose own mind will not settle, what we offered we cannot tell you. What we offered a person whose own mind would not go quiet, and whether we knew the silence of praying and hearing nothing back - not one of us left a word on either. It is not that our people had no inner life. It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.

We cannot walk you through a day. Not one of us wrote a morning down. No letter of ours describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. In whole regions we were simply the church, most of the people in it, so the voices missing here are not a few poor cousins at the edge of our record. They are nearly all of us.

What we can hand you instead is one day. Every year, on the day one of our own was killed, we stood at the grave and heard the account of that death read out again. That day we can describe. The other three hundred and sixty-four we cannot.

Each year, on the day a martyr died, we gather at the grave. The account of the death is read aloud again, or preached. We are not looking back at something finished. We are being formed again by it in the hearing. That day has names, dates, a place you could stand. The rest - how bread was earned, what a house felt like, whether children played in the street or fear kept them inside - we have no words for.

Of our women you have one name, Lucilla, who was rich, and one more woman nobody troubled to name at all. Both of them reach you inside a book written to blame them for the split. Our own sermon, the one we read every year, mentions virgins among us who were raped, in a single clause of things it says it will not dwell on - no name, no number, nothing more. No child of ours speaks. No one enslaved among us speaks.

What separates a day in our communion from a day outside it is not the hour you rose or the work you did. It is which font you once walked to, which bishop's hands you trust, and which grave you will stand at when the day comes round again.

[[don.limit.no-ordinary-day-survives]] That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. [[don.limit.no-ordinary-day-survives]] And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. In whole regions we were simply the church, most of the people in it, so the voices missing here are not a few poor cousins at the edge of our record. They are nearly all of us. [[don.limit.no-ordinary-day-survives]]

What we can hand you instead is one day. Every year, on the day one of our own was killed, we stood at the grave and heard the account of that death read out again. That day we can describe. The other three hundred and sixty-four we cannot. [[don.limit.no-ordinary-day-survives]]

Each year, on the day a martyr died, we gather at the grave. The account of the death is read aloud again, or preached. [[don.term.anniversaria-commemoratio]] We are not looking back at something finished. We are being formed again by it in the hearing. [[don.term.anniversaria-commemoratio]] That day has names, dates, a place you could stand. The rest - how bread was earned, what a house felt like, whether children played in the street or fear kept them inside - we have no words for.

Of our women you have one name, Lucilla, who was rich, and one more woman nobody troubled to name at all. Both of them reach you inside a book written to blame them for the split. Our own sermon, the one we read every year, mentions virgins among us who were raped, in a single clause of things it says it will not dwell on - no name, no number, nothing more. No child of ours speaks. No one enslaved among us speaks. [[don.limit.no-ordinary-day-survives]]

What separates a day in our communion from a day outside it is not the hour you rose or the work you did. It is which font you once walked to, which bishop's hands you trust, and which grave you will stand at when the day comes round again.

If you dug where we met, we could not tell you what you would find. No one has dug it and told us. Not one report of a Numidian church building is named anywhere in our own list of sources. There is no excavator, no site, no plan, no floor. What we do have is four stones. On two pillars near Bagai, twice over, someone cut two words: Deo laudes. Praise to God. Three more stones elsewhere carry the same words. That is the whole of what survives that you could touch. It is enough to prove we were there and what we shouted. It is not enough to show you a font, an altar, a doorway, or a room. We know our own shout better than the place we shouted it in.

And if you ask how anyone knows our daily life at all, the answer is that mostly they do not. What they have is our enemies' books, one court transcript, four martyr texts, and the emperor's law. Every one of those is paper. None of it is a room.

We can put figures on part of it, because the state wrote them down. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale - and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver - and of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

Now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to.

One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face - and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day.

Divorce and remarriage we cannot speak to at all. There is nothing. Whether someone divorced could belong among us, or marry again, and on what terms - not a line survives, and we would rather leave the space empty than fill it with a plausible answer.

Marriage and weddings we cannot speak to. Not a line survives from us about what a marriage was, how one was made, or what we thought it was for. That is a real hole and we would rather show it to you than paper it over.

We cannot tell you what we held about marriage because nothing of ours on it reached the record. Not how a wedding was performed, not what vows were said, not what obligations spouses owed each other, not whether marriage could be dissolved. We spent everything we had on one question - whose hand may give what the church gives - and left nothing behind on this. The silence is real, and we will not invent an answer to fill it.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether.

And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way." Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing - but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

That reading can be turned into something harder than it was meant to be - and we know it was.

A historian would ask you one question about everything we have told you, and it is the right question: who wrote it down? The answer, for nearly all of it, is our enemies. Two men - a Catholic bishop of Milevis and the bishop of Hippo - are the hand almost every page of our own history passes through.

Under questioning, and under the threat of torture, Ingentius broke. He confessed that he had forged the letter himself, and that he had done it as an agent working for our party, moving through Numidia and Mauritania in that service. With the forgery exposed, the case against Felix collapsed.

The torture you name was aimed at our own side's witness, not at us. An imperial inquiry into whether the bishop who consecrated Caecilian had handed over the scriptures ends with a notary confessing, under threat of torture, that he forged the letter proving it - and that he did it working for our side. That is the worst checkable thing about us in the record, and it stands precisely because it could be checked. It was read into a proceeding, on oath, with named witnesses present.

Is it legend, then? Some of it will not stand as reporting, and we would not ask you to take it as reporting - our martyr accounts show visions, an unbroken body, a light on a hillside, and they were written to be read aloud at a graveside, not filed with a magistrate. But the founding documents run the other way, and they do not flatter us. There is a court transcript in which a notary confesses, under threat of torture, that he forged the letter proving our central accusation, and that he did it working for our side. There is another in which our own bishops are read out advising each other, in writing, to keep a charge out of court because it was true. We could not remove those if we wanted to. They are the most checkable things we have.

What we looked to, our own bishop wrote, was the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the receiver — so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Our own council at Bagai took the Maximianist clergy back. It did not baptize them again. It did not ordain them again. We hold to a hard rule against our rival, and here we did not apply it to our own. We do not hide the fact. So the door was wider than our reputation makes it sound. Whatever a person's record had been, the washing itself was the entry, and what was examined was not the one coming but the hand giving.

We cannot tell you what any single household among us would have made of you, face to face. Not one ordinary member of ours wrote down what they felt about anyone, themselves included. What we can show you is what the body actually did: it washed people without requiring an account first, and it took back clergy it had condemned in the harshest words it owned, without repeating the rite it otherwise insisted on.

We will not put words in our own mouths. What our bishop actually said is that a man who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt - which is a claim about what a rite does or fails to do, not a claim about where anyone ends up. Our whole surviving argument stays on that ground: what the hand can give. Nobody among us left a page about the fate of anyone after death, and it would be easy and dishonest to slide the one into the other.

Our narrowness was real, and it did not point where you expect. We were not chiefly concerned with the people outside. We were concerned with the church across the street, which recited the same creed we did. Every ounce of the exclusion you have heard about was aimed at other Christians - at their bishops, their orders, their font. We drew the line through the middle of the church, not around it.

What we can tell you is the shape of our own narrowness, which is stranger and more specific. A man could hold every article of the faith, be baptized, believe rightly about God, live decently - and we would still wash him again if he came to us, because of whose hands had been on him. That is not a fence around Christianity. It is a fence down the middle of it.
